description: Videos per interest with conversational learning cards. Each card has subtitle, body (2-4 short paragraphs), and takeaway.

videos.title: 5 Steps to Build Your Financial Future
videos.creator: Dundee Gouin
videos.description: Dundee Gouin breaks down financial planning into five concrete, actionable steps that anyone can implement regardless of current financial situation. The talk addresses common barriers that prevent people from building wealth, showing that financial security isn't about earning more but about systematically implementing basic principles that compound over time. By focusing on behavioral changes rather than complex investment strategies, Gouin provides a framework that works for people at any income level who are willing to prioritize long-term security over short-term consumption.

videos.title: The Psychology of Money
videos.creator: The Plain Bagel
videos.description: Richard Coffin examines why people make irrational financial decisions even when they understand the logic of good money management, exploring the psychological and behavioral factors that cause intelligent people to consistently act against their own financial interests. The video demonstrates that financial success has less to do with intelligence or knowledge than with controlling behavior and emotions around money. By analyzing common cognitive biases like loss aversion, recency bias, and overconfidence, the video reveals why most people struggle with money despite having access to all the information they need to succeed financially.

cards.title: Pay Yourself First
cards.subtitle: Most people pay bills first and save what's left—but there's never anything left.
body: The fundamental problem with saving what's left over after expenses is that there's never anything left over. The pay-yourself-first principle reverses the order entirely.

By automating savings transfers the moment your paycheck arrives, you treat savings like a bill that can't be skipped rather than a nice-to-have that happens with leftover money. It sounds simple, but it changes everything.
cards.takeaway: Treat savings like a non-negotiable bill, not an afterthought.

cards.title: Emergency Funds Prevent Debt Spirals
cards.subtitle: Without emergency savings, every unexpected expense becomes debt you'll pay off for months at punishing interest.
body: Your car broke down. You used a credit card. Now you're paying 20% interest on a repair. The $1,200 fix ends up costing $1,800 over time.
If another emergency hits before you've paid off the first, you spiral deeper into debt. Emergency funds aren't optional—they're what keep small setbacks from becoming long-term traps.
cards.takeaway: An emergency fund is your first line of defense against debt spirals.

cards.title: Compound Interest Works Both Ways
cards.subtitle: Saving $200 a month at 7% becomes roughly $500k in 40 years. Credit card debt at 20% does the opposite.
body: Compound interest is the most powerful force in personal finance. It works massively in your favor when you're earning it—and catastrophically against you when you're paying it.

When you invest $200 per month at a 7% annual return, time and compounding turn those small contributions into roughly $500,000 over forty years. The same math works against you when you're carrying debt.
cards.takeaway: Compound interest rewards patience and punishes procrastination.

cards.title: Invest in Assets, Not Liabilities
cards.subtitle: Assets put money in your pocket. Liabilities take it out. A new car loses 30% of its value the moment you drive it off the lot.
body: The distinction between assets and liabilities is simple but profound. Assets appreciate or generate income. Liabilities depreciate and cost you money.

When you buy a new car, it loses 20–30% of its value immediately, then continues depreciating while costing you insurance, maintenance, and fuel. That's not to say you shouldn't buy a car—but know what you're buying.
cards.takeaway: Wealth builds when money flows toward assets, not liabilities.

cards.title: Lifestyle Inflation Erases Raises
cards.subtitle: You got a 10% raise. Your rent went up, your car got nicer, subscriptions multiplied. You're not saving more.
body: Lifestyle inflation is the silent killer of wealth building. Income increases translate into spending increases rather than saving increases.

You get a raise and suddenly you're looking at nicer apartments, upgrading your car, adding premium subscriptions, eating out more. Before you know it, your expenses have risen to match your new income.
The fix is simple: decide in advance how much of any raise goes to savings, before lifestyle creeps in.
cards.takeaway: Lock in savings before lifestyle inflation claims your raise.

cards.title: Debt Delays Financial Independence
cards.subtitle: Every dollar you send to debt payments is a dollar that can't compound for decades.
body: When you're paying $1,500 per month on car loans, student debt, and credit cards, that's $18,000 annually that could be invested and compounding.

If you eliminated that debt and invested those payments instead at a 7% return, you'd have nearly $1 million after thirty years. Debt isn't just a monthly burden—it's opportunity cost on a massive scale.
cards.takeaway: Debt is the primary obstacle to financial independence for most people.

cards.title: Financial Literacy Isn't Taught
cards.subtitle: You spent twelve years in school and zero hours on personal finance. You learned by expensive mistakes.
body: The education system systematically fails to teach personal finance. You can graduate with honors having never learned about compound interest, tax-advantaged retirement accounts, or how credit cards work.
People enter adulthood without understanding how to manage money, invest, avoid debt traps, or build wealth. The cost of that gap is paid in real dollars over a lifetime.
cards.takeaway: Financial literacy is rarely taught—so you have to seek it out.

cards.title: Budgeting Reveals Spending Patterns
cards.subtitle: You thought you spent $200 a month on food. You spent $600. Awareness precedes change.
body: The gap between what you think you spend and what you actually spend is usually enormous. Most people estimate $200 per month on food, then track it and discover $600 when you include restaurants, coffee shops, and impulse buys.
Tracking creates dramatic results even without changing behavior at first. You can't change patterns you're not aware of.
cards.takeaway: Track your spending before you try to change it.

cards.title: Retirement Starts Now, Not Later
cards.subtitle: Someone who started saving at 25 will have roughly twice as much at 65 as someone who started at 35.
body: The timing of retirement contributions matters far more than the amount because of compounding over long time horizons.

Someone who starts saving $5,000 annually at age 25 will have roughly twice as much at age 65 as someone who starts at 35, even if they contribute the same amount. Those first ten years have forty years to compound; contributions starting at 35 only have thirty.
cards.takeaway: Start retirement savings as early as you can—time is your biggest asset.

cards.title: Financial Goals Need Specificity
cards.subtitle: Vague goals like 'be rich' don't drive behavior. '$1 million net worth by 50' is actionable.
body: Goals like 'be rich' or 'save more' can't be measured or planned for. When you define a specific target—$1 million net worth by age 50—that goal becomes actionable.
You can work backward to determine exactly how much you need to save monthly and what returns you need to hit. Specificity enables planning by converting wishes into concrete numbers and timelines.
cards.takeaway: Define your financial goals in numbers and dates.
